title: School Year Shut Down: Dedicate the Year Behind
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: As part of his end-of-year "School Year Shut Down" series, Dave shares a colleague's (Martee Lopez-Schmidt's) adaptation of Henry Seton's daily-dedication strategy: a short in-class activity where students dedicate their year's academic work to a person who mattered to them, modeled on a book's dedication page. He walks through the four-step classroom procedure and shares his own example dedication, to his late grandfather, to model the vulnerability and tone he wants students to bring to the exercise.
points: Adapts a "book dedication page" metaphor into a 15-minute end-of-year classroom activity: students dedicate their year's academic labor to a person, living or not, who shaped them.
Provides a simple four-step classroom procedure (brainstorm, write, optionally add a photo, share) that any teacher can run with minimal prep.
Models vulnerability by sharing his own dedication, to his grandfather, whose simple daily affirmation he says he's still processing the impact of as an adult.
Frames the exercise as connecting school to "all of life" rather than treating the two as separate, arguing that end-of-year rituals serve students' whole selves, not just their coursework.
quotes: Here's a simple approach that can work if you've only got a 15-minute time period with your students.
When author's finish the hard work of writing a book, they'll often dedicate the labor to someone. Have you ever noticed those dedication pages at the starts of books?
I want you to think of one person or group — someone alive, someone passed, someone you've known personally, someone you've not — that you'd like to dedicate this past year's academic labors to.

Every time I ever saw him, he would kiss me on the lips and then look me in the eye and say, "I love you and I'm proud of you." That might sound awkward, but it was always so deeply affirming to my soul.
It's just a beautiful idea. It's good for our souls. It acknowledges the reality that school is not all of life, but school can be connected to all of life depending on how we think on it.
